title: Approve Papyrus cloud CLI login from another device without secret handoff
description:
Requested by Ryan for Claude through Kanbus (2026-10-30). This filing authorizes issue records only; implementation and any live identity/backend changes are subsequent work. No production login, deployment, IAM changes, secrets in chat, or direct message to Claude. Dot must operate from cloud/headless Linux without a Mac or AWS CLI. Optional shared auth libraries must not combine the two CLI products. Write executable behavioral specifications before implementation; use fake providers/stores in automated tests, and separately record any approved live evidence.

As an authorized newsroom user, I want to open a URL on another device and approve a waiting cloud CLI, so dot can access my authorized publications securely.

Acceptance criteria:
- Explicit remote login produces a clean HTTPS approval-page URL and waits with bounded polling; no browser or loopback connection to the cloud host is required. No authorization codes, refresh tokens, client secrets or bearer credentials pass through chat or manual copy/paste.
- Do not assume Cognito User Pools implement RFC 8628. Evaluate and document a secured broker or equivalent supported handoff, provider constraints, threat model and deployment prerequisites before implementation. Reuse Google/Cognito identity and existing server authorization; never scrape a browser session or silently use AWS/IAM.
- Bind each transaction to the initiating CLI proof/secret, approved identity, issuer/client, exact publication endpoint and requested account/scope. Single-use redemption, short expiry, denial/cancel states, replay protection, CSRF/state protections, rate limits and bounded backoff are required. Approval must clearly show the requester, target and privileges. Another CLI or altered target cannot redeem approval. The displayed URL is not sufficient to redeem credentials.
- Save the resulting renewable session only in an available approved secure store; preserve current per-site registry and endpoint matching. Test two simultaneous publication logins with separate grants. Reauthorize protected operations server-side.
- Preserve local browser/PKCE login and existing multi-site commands. Pending/denied/expired/network failures are bounded, secret-safe and leave no half-authenticated session. Document cleanup and recovery.

Feature: Remote publication login
  Scenario: Approve from another device
    Given a headless Linux CLI requests login for an authorized publication
    When the user opens the URL on their phone and approves
    Then only the initiating CLI receives a securely stored renewable session for that publication
    And no secret or authorization code passes through chat
  Scenario: Refuse replay and substituted targets
    Given an expired, denied, redeemed or differently bound transaction
    When a CLI attempts redemption
    Then no usable session is issued
  Scenario: Multiple sites stay isolated
    Given two independently approved publication sessions
    When one expires or is revoked
    Then the other remains usable and no request uses the wrong endpoint or account

References: docs/cli-login.md; docs/operator-cli.md; src/papyrus_content/cli_user_auth.py; src/papyrus_content/macos_keychain.py; features_backend/cli-user-auth.feature; existing PPY-236bee (login), PPY-109943 (storage), PPY-829904 (renewal), PPY-3ba3d9 (device delegation, a different grant type). Coordinate with that delegation work rather than treating its human-decision grant as a general login credential.

comments.author: home
comments.text:
Plan (Claude, 2026-10-30; decisions by Ryan in chat).

Decisions: one broker per site (in each site's own backend, approval page on the site's own domain). Cloud machines without a keychain use a memory-only `papyrus auth agent` (see PPY-109943). Same pattern goes to the Cyclotron session as a design note, not shared code.

Why a broker: Cognito does not implement the RFC 8628 device flow, and AWS's `--remote` has the user paste a code back, which this story forbids.

Flow (split secrets):
1. `papyrus login --remote <site>`: the CLI makes a PKCE verifier V and a poll secret P and keeps both. It POSTs to the site broker `/start`: publication, client id, code_challenge S256(V), sha256(P), requester label (host name, CLI version). The broker returns a transaction id T, a short matching code, `https://<site>/cli/approve?t=T`, a poll interval and an expiry (about 10 minutes).
2. The approval page shows the requester, the matching code, the site and "acts as you with your newsroom permissions". Approve sends the browser to Cognito `/oauth2/authorize` (Google) with the transaction's code_challenge, redirect `https://<site>/cli/callback`, and state = T plus a CSRF nonce bound to a browser cookie. Deny and cancel are recorded.
3. `/cli/callback` checks the state and hands the authorization code to the broker for T.
4. The CLI polls `/poll` with T and P and receives the code exactly once (then the record is deleted). It exchanges the code at the Cognito token endpoint with V, and stores the session as a local login would.

Properties: no token or code in chat or copy/paste. The broker never holds a token, and the code it holds briefly is useless without V. The link cannot redeem anything without P. Single use, short expiry, DynamoDB TTL, per-caller rate limits on /start and /poll, bounded polling with slow_down backoff. Each site's broker serves only its own publication and client.

Build:
- Shared site backend: broker Lambda with a function URL (no auth on start/poll; complete/deny need the state/nonce), plus a DynamoDB table with TTL.
- Shared app shell: `/cli/approve` and `/cli/callback` pages.
- Discovery file: optional `remote_login_endpoint` and `remote_callback_uri`.
- CLI: `--remote` on `papyrus login`, using the existing per-site registry and endpoint matching.

Live prerequisite (needs Ryan's approval): add `https://<site>/cli/callback` to each site's Cognito web client callback URLs and deploy the broker.

Order: Gherkin specs plus fake broker/provider tests first, then the backend and pages, then the CLI, then proof on a test publication before any other site.

comments.author: home
comments.text: Plan update (Claude, 2026-10-30). Ryan: the Papyrus and Cyclotron CLI logins work the same way, keeping the best choices from both (no shared code). Kept from this plan: the throttling on both brokers (per-caller rate limits on /start and /poll, slow_down), one broker per deployment with its own function URL and DynamoDB TTL table, /start, /poll, /cli/approve, /cli/callback, and the discovery keys remote_login_endpoint and remote_callback_uri. Added from the Cyclotron plan (AnthusAI/Cyclotron docs/cli-remote-login.md, PR #177): (1) the approval page asks the person to compare the matching code before approving, not only shows it; (2) /poll hands the code over with a conditional delete, so two concurrent polls cannot both receive it; (3) a request carrying both a cookie and a bearer token is refused; (4) the CLI names its secure-store backend explicitly so a library never picks a plaintext one; (5) the client's token settings are read and recorded with the plan and again at release; (6) logout says plainly that an access token the API already accepted stays valid until it expires.
